stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Wandering Stones
stimulus.text:
Scattered across the farm fields and forests of northern Europe and North America lie boulders that do not belong where they are. Some are the size of a car; a few are as large as a house. Many are made of a type of rock entirely different from the bedrock beneath them, such as granite resting on limestone, and some can be traced to outcrops hundreds of kilometers away. For centuries, these misplaced stones posed a puzzle. Something had moved them, and whatever it was had been powerful enough to carry enormous weights across great distances.

Geologists call such boulders erratics, from a Latin word meaning “to wander.” In the early nineteenth century, the most widely accepted explanation for them was a vast flood. According to this view, a great deluge had swept across the continents, and the boulders had been carried along by the rushing water or by icebergs floating on its surface. The flood theory had the advantage of explaining erratics in many places at once, and it fit comfortably with traditional accounts of the earth's history.

Yet the theory had problems. Moving water sorts the material it carries: it drops heavy stones first and carries fine sand and silt farther, leaving neat layers behind. The deposits found alongside many erratics were not sorted at all. Boulders, gravel, sand, and clay lay jumbled together, as if they had been dumped all at once by something that did not distinguish between large and small. In addition, the bedrock in many of these regions was marked by long, parallel scratches, all running in roughly the same direction, as though something heavy had been dragged across it.

The explanation that eventually prevailed came from observers who had spent time in the Alps. There, glaciers could be seen doing exactly what the flood theory struggled to explain. A glacier is a river of ice, and as it creeps downhill it plucks rocks from the land beneath and beside it, carries them along, and grinds them against the bedrock, leaving scratches. When the ice melts, it drops everything it carries in unsorted heaps. Alpine residents had long noticed boulders lying far below the current edges of glaciers and concluded that the ice had once reached much farther.

In the late 1830s, the Swiss-born naturalist Louis Agassiz took this reasoning to a dramatic conclusion. If glaciers in the Alps had once been larger, he argued, then perhaps ice had once covered vast areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including lands that are now temperate. The erratics of northern Europe and North America, the jumbled deposits, the scratched bedrock: all of these could be explained by sheets of ice far larger than any glacier then existing. The idea of an ice age met strong resistance at first. It required imagining a world dramatically different from the present one, and it challenged both the flood theory and the assumption that the earth's climate had always been roughly the same.

Over the following decades, however, evidence accumulated. Geologists mapped the scratches on bedrock and found that they formed consistent patterns radiating outward from a few centers, just as one would expect if great ice sheets had spread from those centers. They traced erratics back to their sources and found that the stones had moved in the directions the scratches indicated. By the end of the nineteenth century, the idea that large parts of the Northern Hemisphere had once been buried under ice was widely accepted.

Today, scientists understand that there was not one ice age but many cycles of glacial advance and retreat over the past few million years. The erratics are reminders of the most recent of these advances, which ended more than ten thousand years ago. Some have become local landmarks, given names and climbed by generations of children; others serve as fence corners in farmers' fields, their history unnoticed. They sit where the ice abandoned them, ordinary-looking stones that once forced people to imagine an entirely different world.

Alpine residents had long noticed boulders lying far below the current edges of glaciers and concluded that the ice had once reached much farther.

In the late 1830s, the Swiss-born naturalist Louis Agassiz took this reasoning to a dramatic conclusion. If glaciers in the Alps had once been larger, he argued, then perhaps ice had once covered vast areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including lands that are now temperate. The erratics of northern Europe and North America, the jumbled deposits, the scratched bedrock: all of these could be explained by sheets of ice far larger than any glacier then existing. The idea of an ice age met strong resistance at first. It required imagining a world dramatically different from the present one, and it challenged both the flood theory and the assumption that the earth's climate had always been roughly the same.

Over the following decades, however, evidence accumulated. Geologists mapped the scratches on bedrock and found that they formed consistent patterns radiating outward from a few centers, just as one would expect if great ice sheets had spread from those centers. They traced erratics back to their sources and found that the stones had moved in the directions the scratches indicated. By the end of the nineteenth century, the idea that large parts of the Northern Hemisphere had once been buried under ice was widely accepted.

Today, scientists understand that there was not one ice age but many cycles of glacial advance and retreat over the past few million years. The erratics are reminders of the most recent of these advances, which ended more than ten thousand years ago. Some have become local landmarks, given names and climbed by generations of children; others serve as fence corners in farmers' fields, their history unnoticed. They sit where the ice abandoned them, ordinary-looking stones that once forced people to imagine an entirely different world.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Wandering Stones
stimulus.text:

Many are made of a type of rock entirely different from the bedrock beneath them, such as granite resting on limestone, and some can be traced to outcrops hundreds of kilometers away. For centuries, these misplaced stones posed a puzzle. Something had moved them, and whatever it was had been powerful enough to carry enormous weights across great distances.
